problemText: Which of the following BEST describes an ecosystem?
choices: All organisms of the same species living in an area
Only the nonliving physical environment of a region
All living organisms in a region together with their nonliving environment and the interactions among them
A group of different species occupying the same habitat, excluding any physical environment
hints: Think about what makes an ecosystem different from a community.

problemText: Which factor MOST strongly determines the type of biome found in a region?
choices: Soil mineral and nutrient content
Distance from the nearest ocean
Historical human land-use patterns
Long-term temperature and precipitation patterns
hints: Biomes are classified by their dominant climate, not their soils or history.

problemText: Which of the following is a characteristic unique to the tundra biome?
choices: Receives more than 200 cm of rainfall each year
Has a layer of permanently frozen subsoil called permafrost
Supports a dense canopy of broad-leaved deciduous trees
Is found only in equatorial regions near sea level
hints: The tundra is the coldest biome — think about what happens to subsoil that never fully thaws.

problemText: A biologist surveys a region that receives less than 25 cm of precipitation per year. Daytime temperatures regularly exceed 45°C, while nighttime temperatures drop near or below freezing. Which biome is the biologist MOST likely in?
choices: Tropical rainforest
Temperate deciduous forest
Desert
Boreal forest (taiga)
hints: Extreme temperature swings combined with very low precipitation define one particular biome.

problemText: Chaparral (Mediterranean shrubland) plants such as manzanita and chamise are adapted to periodic fire PRIMARILY because fire:
choices: Increases soil salinity, which these plants tolerate better than their competitors
Clears dead woody material and releases locked-up nutrients, and these species resprout from deep roots or germinate from fire-stimulated seeds
Lowers average summer temperatures, creating favorable germination conditions
Drives away competing herbivores, reducing grazing pressure on surviving shrubs
hints: Consider how fire affects nutrient cycling and the recovery mechanisms of fire-adapted shrubs.

problemText: As you climb a tall tropical mountain, you pass through vegetation zones that closely resemble the sequence from tropical forest near the equator to tundra near the poles. This pattern is BEST explained by:
choices: Island biogeography — isolated mountaintop habitats attract species from distant biomes
The competitive exclusion principle causing low-altitude species to displace high-altitude ones
Altitudinal zonation, in which decreasing temperature with increasing elevation produces biome-like vegetation zones analogous to latitudinal biome shifts
Ecological succession proceeding faster at higher elevations due to lower competition
hints: Temperature drops roughly 6°C for every 1,000 m gained in elevation, mimicking the cooling at higher latitudes.

problemText: Which process converts atmospheric nitrogen gas (N₂) into a form — such as ammonium (NH₄⁺) — that plants can absorb from the soil?
choices: Nitrification
Denitrification
Assimilation
Nitrogen fixation
hints: 'Fixing' nitrogen means converting it from an atmospheric gas into a biologically usable compound.

problemText: In the nitrogen cycle, nitrifying bacteria perform which conversion?
choices: N₂ gas → ammonium (NH₄⁺)
Ammonium (NH₄⁺) → nitrite, then nitrate (NO₃⁻)
Nitrate (NO₃⁻) → atmospheric N₂
Organic nitrogen in dead matter → ammonium (NH₄⁺)
hints: The prefix 'nitrify' means to form nitrate — these bacteria oxidize ammonium stepwise.

problemText: A key difference between the phosphorus cycle and the nitrogen cycle is that the phosphorus cycle:
choices: Relies heavily on an atmospheric gas reservoir to store and redistribute phosphorus globally
Requires specialized decomposers to break phosphorus out of organic matter before plants can use it
Lacks a significant atmospheric component; phosphorus cycles primarily through rocks, soil, and water
Completes a full cycle much faster than the nitrogen cycle because reactions are simpler
hints: There is no gas-phase form of phosphorus in the environment, unlike nitrogen (N₂).

problemText: Denitrification is ecologically important PRIMARILY because it:
choices: Adds plant-available ammonium to nitrogen-depleted soils
Returns reactive nitrogen to the atmosphere as N₂ gas, preventing indefinite accumulation of nitrates in soils and waterways
Transforms atmospheric N₂ into ammonium that plant roots can directly absorb
Breaks down urea and other animal waste products into usable ammonium
hints: Denitrification is the step that closes the nitrogen cycle — it removes reactive nitrogen from the ecosystem.

problemText: The widespread use of synthetic nitrogen fertilizers in agriculture MOST directly disrupts the nitrogen cycle by:
choices: Reducing populations of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in farm soils
Converting atmospheric N₂ directly into oxygen, altering air composition
Introducing large quantities of reactive nitrogen that leach into waterways and promote eutrophication
Lowering soil temperature, which slows decomposition and nutrient cycling
hints: Think about what happens when excess fertilizer washes off fields into streams and lakes.

problemText: In most freshwater lakes, algal growth is primarily limited by the availability of which nutrient?
choices: Phosphorus, because it is naturally scarce in freshwater relative to the amount of nitrogen available
Nitrogen, because cyanobacteria cannot fix enough N₂ to meet total algal demand
Carbon dioxide, because aquatic producers must compete for dissolved CO₂
Iron, because iron-deficient photosynthesis limits most temperate freshwater algae
hints: Freshwater systems tend to have more dissolved nitrogen than phosphorus — so phosphorus runs short first.

problemText: Which biological process is PRIMARILY responsible for removing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and incorporating carbon into organic molecules?
choices: Cellular respiration
Combustion
Photosynthesis
Decomposition
hints: Producers use sunlight to convert CO₂ and water into sugars, fixing atmospheric carbon.

problemText: What role do decomposers (bacteria and fungi) play in the carbon cycle?
choices: They fix atmospheric CO₂ into organic compounds, functioning as a second class of producer
They break down dead organic matter and release its stored carbon back into the atmosphere as CO₂ through respiration
They permanently lock carbon into deep soil organic matter, increasing long-term carbon storage
They transfer carbon from ocean sediments directly to terrestrial ecosystems
hints: Decomposers are heterotrophs — they respire as they break down dead material, releasing CO₂.

problemText: In the water cycle, transpiration specifically refers to:
choices: Water evaporating directly from the surfaces of lakes, rivers, and oceans
The downward movement of water through soil into underground aquifers
Water vapor released through the stomata (pores) in plant leaves
Precipitation soaking into the ground rather than running off the surface
hints: Transpiration is the plant-mediated 'T' in 'evapotranspiration.'

problemText: Which of the following represents the LARGEST long-term reservoir of carbon on Earth?
choices: Living terrestrial vegetation (plant biomass)
Fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas) in Earth's crust
Soil organic matter and peat deposits
The ocean, including dissolved inorganic carbon and marine carbonate sediments
hints: Think in geologic terms — where has carbon been accumulating for hundreds of millions of years?

problemText: Widespread deforestation MOST directly affects the carbon cycle by:
choices: Increasing the rate of nitrogen fixation in newly cleared soils
Decreasing ocean salinity as organic carbon washes into the sea
Removing a major terrestrial carbon sink and releasing stored carbon as CO₂ through burning and decomposition
Accelerating the water cycle by increasing surface runoff
hints: Forests act as carbon sinks — removing them converts that sink into a carbon source.

problemText: During a prolonged drought, plants close their stomata to conserve water. Closing stomata MOST directly affects both the carbon cycle and the water cycle simultaneously by:
choices: Increasing photosynthesis rates because CO₂ accumulates inside the leaf when stomata are sealed
Reducing transpiration AND reducing CO₂ uptake, simultaneously slowing local water recycling and carbon fixation
Increasing cellular respiration rates to compensate for reduced photosynthesis output
Stimulating greater root uptake of groundwater to maintain both turgor pressure and photosynthesis
hints: Stomata are the gateway for both water vapor to exit and CO₂ to enter — closing them restricts both fluxes at once.

problemText: Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) in an ecosystem is BEST defined as:
choices: The energy remaining in producers after all consumer respiration losses are subtracted
The total carbon fixed by herbivores and carnivores combined
The total rate of photosynthesis by producers — all energy captured from sunlight before any respiratory losses
The energy stored in producers and available to herbivores after plant respiration is subtracted
hints: 'Gross' means total before subtracting anything — it is the full photosynthesis output of producers.

problemText: A forest ecosystem has a GPP of 8,000 kcal/m²/yr. Producers use 3,200 kcal/m²/yr in cellular respiration. What is the Net Primary Productivity (NPP) of this forest?
choices: 11,200 kcal/m²/yr
8,000 kcal/m²/yr
3,200 kcal/m²/yr
4,800 kcal/m²/yr
hints: NPP = GPP − Respiration. Subtract what the plants use for their own metabolism.

problemText: A grassland ecosystem has a Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) of 6,500 kcal/m²/yr. Producers use 2,100 kcal/m²/yr in cellular respiration. What is the Net Primary Productivity (NPP) of this grassland, in kcal/m²/yr?
hints: NPP = GPP − Respiration.

problemText: Approximately 90% of energy is lost at each trophic level, leaving only about 10% to transfer to the next level. This loss occurs PRIMARILY because:
choices: Predators selectively consume the least nutritious prey, wasting most available energy
Decomposers intercept the majority of energy before higher trophic levels can access it
Most energy consumed by an organism is used in cellular respiration or lost as heat, leaving only a small fraction stored as new biomass
Solar energy reaching each successive trophic level is physically reduced by 90% due to canopy shading
hints: Think about what organisms do with most of the energy they ingest — they respire it to power life functions, generating heat.

problemText: A prairie ecosystem has producers (grasses) with 500,000 kcal/m²/yr of energy available. Assuming 10% trophic efficiency at each level, calculate the energy available (in kcal/m²/yr) to secondary consumers (carnivores that eat the herbivores).
hints: Apply 10% twice: producers to herbivores, then herbivores to secondary consumers.

problemText: A region is deciding how to allocate its cropland. Scenario A feeds the population directly on grain (plants). Scenario B raises cattle on that same grain and then feeds the population on beef. Assuming 10% trophic efficiency, Scenario A can support how many times MORE people than Scenario B from the same grain harvest?
choices: 10 times more people
2 times more people
100 times more people
The same number of people, because caloric content is equivalent at each step
hints: In Scenario B, only 10% of grain energy reaches humans via beef. In Scenario A, 100% of grain energy goes directly to humans.

problemText: A food web differs from a simple food chain in that a food web:
choices: Shows only one linear feeding pathway from a single producer to a single top predator
Includes only decomposers and primary producers in its diagram
Represents multiple, interconnected feeding relationships among all species in an ecosystem
Tracks the flow of water and mineral nutrients rather than energy
hints: Most real ecosystems have many overlapping food chains — a food web captures all of them simultaneously.

problemText: In a simple food chain — grasses → rabbits → hawks — at which trophic level are the rabbits?
choices: First trophic level (primary producer)
Second trophic level (primary consumer)
Third trophic level (secondary consumer)
Fourth trophic level (tertiary consumer)
hints: Count steps from the producer: grasses are level 1, so the next organism in the chain is level 2.

problemText: In a food web, a plant-eating insect is eliminated by a pesticide application. Which of the following effects is MOST likely to occur first?
choices: The plants the insect fed on immediately go extinct due to unrelated competition
Top carnivores in the food web immediately double their population size
Populations of insect-eating birds decline because their food source has been reduced
Decomposers rapidly increase activity to process the extra dead insect biomass
hints: Follow the energy pathway upward: the insect feeds birds — remove the insect and the birds lose a key food source.

problemText: Sea otters prey on sea urchins; sea urchins consume kelp. When sea otters were hunted nearly to extinction, urchin populations exploded and kelp forests were destroyed. Sea otters are called a keystone species because:
choices: Their removal causes a disproportionately large change in ecosystem structure relative to their own biomass or abundance
They are the most abundant organism in the kelp forest and directly support the most food chains
They are apex predators with no natural predators of their own in this system
They fix atmospheric nitrogen that fertilizes kelp and supports the entire food web
hints: 'Keystone' describes outsized impact — a relatively low-biomass species whose loss triggers major ecosystem change.

problemText: A salt marsh food chain is: phytoplankton → zooplankton → small fish → osprey. Phytoplankton fix 200,000 kcal/m²/yr. Assuming 10% trophic efficiency at each step, how much energy (in kcal/m²/yr) is available to ospreys?
hints: Apply the 10% rule three times moving from phytoplankton up to ospreys.

problemText: When wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park, elk populations declined and shifted their grazing patterns. Riverbank vegetation recovered, stabilizing stream banks and altering river flow. This sequence BEST illustrates:
choices: Primary succession initiated by the arrival of an apex predator in a previously bare habitat
A trophic cascade in which a change at one trophic level ripples through the food web and alters the physical environment
Competitive exclusion between wolves and elk competing for the same food resources
Mutualism between wolves and riparian vegetation providing each other with benefits
hints: Wolves changed elk behavior, which changed plant growth, which changed rivers — each effect cascaded downward from the top predator.
